title: Making a roguelike game for my bf bday
author: Cookies-n-Cream-
selftext:
So my bf is physically disabled. He loves tennis but he can barely move out of his bed these days. I had this crazy idea of vibe coding a tennis roguelike game with a skill tree, unlockable items, different upgradable weapons and upgrades and a shop during the run that doesn't convert to other runs. 

There are waves of mobs to fight until the boss fights, which are tennis games with a little spice. Each boss has different mechanics and they are based of his irl friends with plenty of easter eggs and dialogues in between. 

I have been working on it for three days straight now and do have a base model. I did use up my 100 codex astra weekly limit already however. I have three weeks to finish this until his bday. It is already playable but making it challenging, satisfying and enjoyable with a reasonable progression curve is so hard.

I am disabled myself so actually play testing is honestly the biggest issue for me. I have little experience with roguelikes but I did ask plenty of questions while he was gaming them to ask what he likes about it. I do plan on sending this to his best friend for play testing eventually, but I want it to be somewhat finished atp. 

Does anyone have any tips and ideas on balancing or just in genrral on this mammuth project? I may have aimed a little bit high but now I am super committed and i vested quite a bit of money already

comments.author: Low-Bad7547
comments.body: Are you using your own engine or a premade engine?

replies.author: Alarmed-Quail7617
replies.body: You've made it 1000x harder on yourself, tell your engine to code it in webgl2 instead then just wrap it with electron if you want/need a desktop exe

replies.author: Alarmed-Quail7617
replies.body: You get 100x the freedom without the bullshit of needing to deal with a third party engine

replies.author: Low-Bad7547
replies.body: Eh, until you need to build a entity system

replies.author: Alarmed-Quail7617
replies.body: Not at all a problem lol

replies.author: Low-Bad7547
replies.body: Really depends what you are doing because your entity system dictates some tradeoff you can't ignore.

replies.author: Alarmed-Quail7617
replies.body: I'm really curious what limitations you think exist because i promise you that it is far better than you think. I this as someone with a $100k game recently built on that engine

replies.author: Low-Bad7547
replies.body:
Sure: ECS vs inheritance system directly impacts your performance and extendability (even design wise) of your entities. And inside ECS you can have archetypes vs sparse sets (google it) that have their own tradeoffs, and no amount of money you throw at it will change the basic physics that dictate how these work (how stuff from ram is fetched and computed).   
If you system doesn't need these tradeoffs: you are safe. If you prefer performance vs understandability vs extendability you have to make the tradeoff, and you can't make the tradeoff unless you understand at a basic level what you are giving up for what.

replies.author: Alarmed-Quail7617
replies.body: I'm able to have stable 120+ FPS for 1000s of players with 500+ units on the screen though. I think you really underestimate what webgl2 can do now.

replies.author: Low-Bad7547
replies.body: I'll look into it, I'm saying that in the limit you can't escape tradeoffs. In the limit. And making those tradeoffs will force you to have a basic understanding what you are giving up for what.

comments.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
comments.body:
Since playtesting is the hard part, I’d send his friend a rough five-minute build now, before it feels finished. Ask them to note where they die, get stuck, or stop knowing what to do. One wave, one upgrade and one friend-boss can make a complete little birthday game; the rest can be bonuses if there’s time.



If you can discreetly find out which controls and session length are comfortable for him, build around those. Optional slower speed or remapping might help, depending on what he uses. This is a lovely gift idea.

replies.author: Cookies-n-Cream-
replies.body:
How do I go about sending someone a playtest file? Do i just send them the current folder of the game? This is honestly my first time doing a game besides coding tik tak to one time.

He really likes games the have insane level of depth honestly. He spends hours and hours on runs and loves trying out different build combinations and unlocking random achievments. Currently he is addicted to ballxpit (I think it was called)

replies.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
replies.body:
Since you’re using Godot, you can send a playable export instead of the project folder. If your friend uses Windows:



1. In Godot, open Project → Export, click Add, and choose Windows Desktop. If Godot says export templates are missing, install the matching templates when prompted.

2. Choose Export Project and save it in a new folder. If it creates both an .exe and a .pck, keep them together. Zip that folder and send it privately. Try opening the exported .exe yourself first.



Godot’s guide has screenshots: [https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/exporting\_projects.html](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/exporting_projects.html)



And that helps about the depth! You could have the friend test whether two early upgrade combinations feel different, even in a short build. Does your friend play on Windows or another platform?

replies.author: Cookies-n-Cream-
replies.body: Thanks that helps! All of us use windows. So that makes it easier. His friend plays on controller though. Not sure if it would be hard to implement that

replies.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
replies.body:
Good news: Godot has built-in controller support, though the work depends on how your current controls are written. A small first test:



1. Open Project → Project Settings → Input Map. Find the actions your game uses for movement and attack. Add the controller’s stick directions or D-pad to the movement actions, and a controller button to attack, alongside the existing keys.

2. Connect the controller and test just movement and attack in the game. If your code reads individual keyboard keys instead of named actions, you may need to change that code first. Then check whether the menus can be navigated too.



Godot’s guide shows the mapping steps: [https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/getting\_started/first\_3d\_game/02.player\_input.html](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/getting_started/first_3d_game/02.player_input.html)



No need to solve every control at once—getting one movement action working is a good start.

comments.author: VortexAssetStudio
comments.body: That is honestly a super cool gift idea. With only 3 weeks and limited playtesting, don't stress about tweaking tiny numbers like +5% or +10% stats. Just make each tier feel noticeably stronger right away, like faster ball speed, splitting the ball, or adding elemental trails. Even if a combo ends up a bit broken, feeling overpowered in a birthday roguelike is way more fun than feeling weak.Also, since he loves deep builds, try to make the upgrade icons really distinct in shape and color so he can read the shop at a glance without reading a wall of text every wave (I make a lot of RPG and roguelike icons myself and clear silhouettes make a huge difference). A simple game speed slider in the pause menu like 75% or 100% would also let him play comfortably on tired days without you having to rebalance the whole game. Good luck, he is going to love it!

replies.author: Cookies-n-Cream-
replies.body: The game speed slider sounds so interesting! Thanks for the input! I will keep this in mind for sure

replies.author: VortexAssetStudio
replies.body: Glad that helps! Another super easy trick for tired days is adding a toggle for "auto-swing" when the ball gets in range, so he can focus purely on positioning and aiming his shots without spamming buttons. If you need any quick visual ideas for how to separate your weapon tiers or shop upgrades by color and silhouette, feel free to peek at some of the icon sets on my profile for inspiration. Best of luck with the deadline, you got this!

comments.author: LatentFactorDev
comments.body: Build a quick headless script to simulate a few hundred runs and log where the player dies most. You can also add a hidden debug menu for enemy health and ball speed so your playtester can tweak the numbers live and tell you what feels fair.
